statement: In middle-aged Danish adults followed for about 15 years (55,917 people aged 50 to 64 at the start, 1993 to 1997), drinking every day compared with drinking on two to four days a week, with the weekly amount (in 12-g drinks), smoking, education and waist size taken into account, is associated with a higher risk of a register diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis in men, but not clearly in women, in one cohort study (Askgaard et al., 2015; no funding stated, no conflicts declared). In men, 171 of 7276 who drank daily and 27 of 9165 who drank on two to four days a week were diagnosed (about 2 in 100 against 3 in 1,000; editors' calculation), but those who drank daily also drank more (median 26 against 8.9 drinks a week): the hazard ratio for daily drinking was 8.29 (95% CI 5.52–12.4) adjusted for age, 4.83 (3.20–7.29) with amount added and 3.65 (2.39–5.55) with smoking, education and waist size as well, while drinking on five or six days a week did not differ clearly from two to four (1.43, 0.84–2.43). In women, 30 of 3931 who drank daily and 15 of 9481 who drank on two to four days a week were diagnosed (about 8 in 1,000 against 2 in 1,000; editors' calculation); with amount and the other factors taken into account, daily drinking gave 1.73 (0.85–3.52) and drinking on five or six days 2.30 (1.14–4.67), with no trend across frequencies (P = 0.14), and the extra risk per weekly drink was largest in women who drank least often (1.09 per drink, against 1.05 in women who drank daily). How often and how much people drank were closely linked (correlation 0.77 in men and 0.85 in women), people who drank daily drank somewhat more even within the same amount category, and the authors say this makes the two hard to separate; drinking was asked about once, at the start, and binge drinking could not be studied. A 2019 review reports, for this cohort, daily drinking against two to four days a week at the same weekly amount as 2.25 (1.68–3.00) in men and 1.28 (0.82–2.02) in women, figures that are not in the cohort paper's main text, and, for a large British cohort of women who drank (the Million Women Study, not read here), 1.61 (1.40–1.85) for daily against non-daily drinking with amount and beverage taken into account, and 0.69 (0.62–0.77) for drinking with meals against outside meals (Roerecke et al., 2019). The cohort's authors advise people who drink daily to drink less often, although no change in drinking was observed in the study. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In one Danish study of 55,917 people aged 50 to 64, men who drank every day were diagnosed with alcohol-related cirrhosis about 3.7 times as often as men who drank on two to four days a week, after taking into account how much they drank, smoking, schooling and waist size. Women showed no clear pattern. But people who drank every day also drank more, and the study could not fully separate how often from how much. A review reported that, in a large British study of women, daily drinking was linked to 1.6 times the risk of drinking on fewer days, and drinking with meals to a lower risk. The Danish study could not look at drinking a lot on a few days (binge drinking).
population: Danish-born adults aged 50 to 64 at entry (1993 to 1997) in the Diet, Cancer and Health cohort, followed to 2011 (26,696 men, 29,221 women); and, second-hand, women in the UK Million Women Study
exposure: Drinking every day (self-reported once, at baseline), with the weekly amount in 12-g drinks taken into account
comparator: Drinking on two to four days a week (Danish cohort); drinking on fewer than seven days a week (Million Women Study, as reported in a review)
outcome: First register diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis (hospital or death records); cirrhosis in the Million Women Study as reported in the review
magnitude: Askgaard et al. 2015, daily against two to four days a week (HR, 95% CI): men 8.29 (5.52–12.4) adjusted for age, 4.83 (3.20–7.29) for age and amount, 3.65 (2.39–5.55) for age, amount, smoking, education and waist; five to six days 1.43 (0.84–2.43); trend P < 0.001. Women 5.01 (2.69–9.31), 1.6 (0.81–3.30) and 1.73 (0.85–3.52); five to six days 2.30 (1.14–4.67); trend P = 0.14. Crude: men 171 of 7276 daily and 27 of 9165 at two to four days; women 30 of 3931 and 15 of 9481. Per weekly drink: men 1.02 (less than one day a week) to 1.05 (daily); women 1.09 to 1.05. Spearman r between frequency and amount 0.77 (men), 0.85 (women). Roerecke et al. 2019 (as reported): Danish cohort 2.25 (1.68–3.00) men, 1.28 (0.82–2.02) women; Million Women Study daily against non-daily 1.61 (1.40–1.85), with meals against outside meals 0.69 (0.62–0.77), daily and outside meals 2.47 (1.96–3.11).

evidence.locator: Introduction, last paragraph; Materials and methods › Study population; Information on alcohol consumption; Statistical analysis, 1st and 6th paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Danish Diet, Cancer and Health cohort: Danish-born men and women aged 50 to 64 invited from December 1993 to May 1997; 55,917 participants analysed. Weekly amounts of beer (330 ml bottles), wine (125 ml glasses) and liquor (30 ml drinks) converted to standard drinks of 12 g of ethanol; drinking frequency in seven categories from never to daily; recalled amounts at ages 20–29, 30–39, 40–49 and 50–59; all from one baseline questionnaire. Cox models with age as the time axis, adjusted for smoking (never, former, under or over 10 g of tobacco a day), education and waist circumference, all stratified by sex. Only average amount and frequency were recorded, so binge drinking could not be explored.

Drinking frequency was highly correlated with baseline amount (Spearman r = 0.77 in men, 0.85 in women). Median weekly amount: men drinking two to four days a week 8.9 drinks (5th–95th percentile 3.6–13), men drinking daily 26 (9.4–60); women 6.6 (3.0–19) and 19 (7.3–40).

evidence.locator: Table 1, Cohort row (p. 3); Table 2, Men rows (p. 4); Results › Alcohol drinking frequency, 2nd paragraph (p. 4)
evidence.extracted: Men: 7276 drank daily and 9165 on two to four days a week (Table 1). Against two to four days a week (27 cases in 135,573 person-years), daily drinking (171 cases in 103,820 person-years) had HR 8.29 (95% CI 5.52–12.4) adjusted for age, 4.83 (3.20–7.29) for age and amount, and 3.65 (2.39–5.55) for age, amount, smoking, education and waist; fully adjusted, five to six days 1.43 (0.84–2.43), one day 1.30 (0.59–2.87), less than one day 1.34 (0.67–2.67), current abstainers 10.0 (4.32–23.0); trend among people who drank P < 0.001. Editors' calculation: 171 of 7276 men drinking daily (about 2.4 in 100) and 27 of 9165 drinking two to four days a week (about 3 in 1,000) were diagnosed over the follow-up; crude rates 165 and 20 per 100,000 person-years.

evidence.locator: Table 1, Cohort row (p. 3); Table 2, Women rows (p. 4); Results › Alcohol drinking frequency, 2nd paragraph (p. 4)
evidence.extracted: Women: 3931 drank daily and 9481 on two to four days a week (Table 1). Against two to four days a week (15 cases in 144,603 person-years), fully adjusted: daily 1.73 (95% CI 0.85–3.52; 30 cases in 58,414 person-years), five to six days 2.30 (1.14–4.67), one day 0.81 (0.29–2.24; the text gives 0.73, 0.27–2.01, the age-adjusted value), less than one day 1.45 (0.71–2.96), current abstainers 4.03 (0.91–17.8); trend P = 0.14. Daily drinking was 5.01 (2.69–9.31) adjusted for age only and 1.6 (0.81–3.30) with amount added. Editors' calculation: 30 of 3931 women drinking daily (about 8 in 1,000) and 15 of 9481 drinking two to four days a week (about 2 in 1,000) were diagnosed.

evidence.locator: Table 3; Results › Alcohol drinking frequency, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: HR per additional weekly drink, by frequency, adjusted for smoking, education and waist: men 1.02 (95% CI 1.01–1.03) at less than one day a week, 1.03 (1.02–1.05) at one to four days, 1.03 (1.02–1.03) at five to six days and 1.05 (1.04–1.05) daily; women 1.09 (1.05–1.13), 1.06 (1.03–1.10), 1.08 (1.06–1.09) and 1.05 (1.04–1.06); the slopes differed by frequency (men P < 0.0001, women P = 0.0007).

Within each category of amount, people drinking daily drank somewhat more on average than those drinking less often, which the authors say makes it difficult to separate the effects of drinking frequency and amount (Supplementary Table 5, not on file).

evidence.locator: Discussion › Comparison with other studies, 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors read their results as confirming that daily drinking increases the risk in men, compared with less frequent drinking; among women they report raised risks at less than one day a week and at five or six days, which they suggest may reflect problem drinking or information bias; their implications are some gain from cutting down regardless of lifetime intake, and advice to people who drink daily to drink less often. No change in drinking was observed in the study (editors' note).

Drinking pattern, single studies as reported in the review: daily drinking against drinking on 2–4 days a week at the same weekly intake, men RR 2.25 (1.68–3.00), women 1.28 (0.82–2.02) (Danish cohort); among women who drank, daily against non-daily drinking 1.61 (1.40–1.85), with meals against outside meals 0.69 (0.62–0.77), daily and outside meals together 2.47 (1.96–3.11), adjusted for amount and beverage type (Million Women Study).

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_askgaard_2015 (ROBINS-E high overall): frequency and amount are correlated (r = 0.77 and 0.85) and adjusting for a self-reported amount removed more than half of the men's age-adjusted excess, so residual confounding by amount is likely; one baseline report for about 15 years; the label 'alcoholic' depends on the drinking being known, so recognised daily drinking may be coded alcoholic more often. The Million Women Study figures are second-hand (card sc_roerecke_2019) and not appraised here.

inconsistency.note: Men and women differ in the Danish cohort (women: no trend, highest at five to six days, steepest per-drink slope in women who drank least often); the British women's cohort, as reported, finds a higher risk with daily drinking; and the 2019 review gives different figures for the Danish cohort (2.25 and 1.28) from those in the cohort paper (3.65 and 1.73).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: daily drinking against two to four days a week in Danish adults aged 50 to 64.

imprecision.note: 85 cases in women (30 among those drinking daily); the women's interval for daily drinking includes 1 (0.85–3.52).

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is rated down one level each for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision, which is below the floor, so very low. Rated as worded: an association of daily drinking with alcoholic cirrhosis at a given self-reported amount, in men in one cohort; the study cannot separate frequency from amount and says nothing about binge drinking. Status mixed: in women the Danish cohort finds no clear pattern while the British cohort, reported second-hand, finds a higher risk with daily drinking; in men there is one study.
